Testart v Testart (No 3)

22 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1558Tribunal reviewVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.
Key holding

A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

Elizabeth Mitkovski v Certis Security Australia

22 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4115Employment & workplace
Ms Mitkovski, a part-time Aviation Screening Officer at Sydney Airport, sought flexible working arrangements to accommodate her caring responsibilities and disputed Certis Security Australia’s refusals of two requests. The Fair Work Commission considered whether Certis had discussed and genuinely tried to reach agreement, had regard to the consequences of refusal, and refused on reasonable business grounds under s 65A(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).
Key holding

A refusal of a flexible working arrangement request is supported by reasonable business grounds where the employer’s reasons are rational and sound and related to its operational requirements and obligations.

I find that the reasons relied upon by Certis constitute reasonable business grounds for the refusal of the requests. Each reason is rational and sound, and related to the Respondent's operational requirements and obligations.

Mr Johnathon Burr v The Trustee for Cornerstone Labour Hire Unit Trust

22 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4121Employment & workplace
Mr Burr’s host assignment with CEVA Logistics ended and he brought an unfair dismissal application against his labour-hire employer, Cornerstone. The Commission had to decide whether Cornerstone dismissed him or whether only his host placement ended; because Cornerstone kept him on its books and sought alternative work, the application was dismissed.
Key holding

Where a labour-hire employee’s host placement ends but the labour-hire employer remains ready and actively attempts to redeploy the employee, the employment has not been terminated on the employer’s initiative and there is no dismissal under s 386(1).

Under s 386(1), a person is considered dismissed if their employment with the employer has been terminated on the employer's initiative. It follows that if the employment continues or if the employer is actively seeking to find alternative work for the employee, there has been no dismissal.

Madana Harrop v Maryborough District Health Service

22 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4112Employment & workplace
Ms Harrop lodged an unfair dismissal application 16 days late after her union, the ANMF, failed to transmit a legal referral due to an automated email system error. The Fair Work Commission accepted representative error as a reasonable explanation, found exceptional circumstances and granted an extension of time. The merits of the unfair dismissal claim have not yet been determined.
Key holding

Where an applicant is blameless and reasonably relies on their representative, a delay caused by the representative’s administrative or system error can be an acceptable explanation for the whole delay and support a finding of exceptional circumstances under s 394(3).

In this case, the reason for the delay was the error of the ANMF, and it is in my view reasonable for the Applicant to have relied on the ANMF's advice that referral would have been made to her legal representatives to pursue an unfair dismissal application. The Applicant should not be disadvantaged because the ANMF experienced a system error in processing of the legal referral.

Stephanie Tranquille v New Beginnings Network

22 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4113Employment & workplaceTax
This was an application by New Beginnings Network to vary an unfair dismissal compensation order so that it could pay $5,025 by instalments of $50 per week, citing financial hardship. The Fair Work Commission refused the amount sought but varied the order to allow 10 weekly instalments of $502.50, with superannuation payable on the original due date.
Key holding

Under s 393 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission has a broad discretion to permit unfair dismissal compensation to be paid by instalments, exercised by weighing the respondent’s business needs and likely compliance against the applicant’s need to access compensation within a reasonable period.

In McCarron, James v Commercial Facilities Management Pty Ltd T/A CFM Air Conditioning Pty Ltd [2013] FWC 3577 in ordering that compensation be paid in instalments Bissett C said that when considering the time period for the instalment payments to be made the business needs of the Respondent must be weighed against the needs of the Applicant to access the compensation.

Yuanyuan (Denise) Wang v Hk Calibration Technologies Pty Ltd

21 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 3891Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission determined a s.365 application by Ms Yuanyuan (Denise) Wang against HK Calibration Technologies Pty Ltd. It upheld the employer’s jurisdictional objection, finding Ms Wang resigned but was not “dismissed” under s.386(1)(b) of the Fair Work Act 2009 because the employer’s conduct was not intended to end employment and did not leave her with no effective or real choice but to resign. The application was dismissed.
Key holding

For a resignation to be a dismissal under s.386(1)(b), the employer’s conduct must be intended to bring employment to an end or make resignation the probable result, leaving the employee no effective or real choice but to resign.

The test to be applied here is whether the employer engaged in the conduct with the intention of bringing the employment to an end or whether termination of the employment was the probably result of the employer's conduct such that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

Communications, Electrical, Electronic, Energy, Information, Postal, Plumbing and Allied Services Union of Australia (128V) v Ausgrid

21 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4082Employment & workplace
The ETU brought a s 739 dispute against Ausgrid over whether Leading Hands performing Emergency Response Coordinator (ERC) on-call duties in Newcastle/Lower Hunter should be paid higher duties at Level 1 of the D2 Field Supervisor band. The Commission found ERC work overlapped with the Leading Hand role and was not the work of a higher-band Field Supervisor, so clause 13 did not apply. It declined to dismiss for want of a live dispute but answered the formulated question “no”.
Key holding

A Leading Hand performing ERC duties is not entitled to higher duties pay under clause 13 because ERC work overlaps with and is contemplated by the Leading Hand role rather than being the responsibilities and duties of a higher-band Field Supervisor Role.

For the reasons set out above, I am not persuaded that the work performed by an ERC is to be regarded as that of a Field Supervisor and not that of a Leading Hand. Rather, I accept Mr Richardson's evidence that there is an overlap between the Roles when it comes to emergency response, and that such overlap is a feature of the R&P Framework.

Mr Gabriel Roccisano v Chop Shop Post Pty Ltd

21 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4091Employment & workplace
Mr Roccisano applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy after being notified of his dismissal by Chop Shop Post Pty Ltd on 4 November 2025. His application, filed on 12 December 2025, was out of time on either possible calculation of the end date. Deputy President Butler refused to extend time, finding that the medical evidence did not establish incapacity to lodge and that distress, financial pressure and ignorance of the 21-day limit were not exceptional circumstances.
Key holding

For the purposes of s 394(3), the distress inherent in losing a job is not of itself an exceptional circumstance, and neither is an asserted psychological condition exceptional unless it is shown to have incapacitated the applicant from lodging within time.

As the cause of action is founded on something as inherently distressing as job loss, distress per se cannot be considered exceptional.

Ms Vikki Turner v Ithaca Crystals Pty Ltd

21 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4080Employment & workplace
Ms Turner lodged an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Her former employer asserted she was not protected because it was a small business and she had not completed the minimum employment period. Ms Turner sought to amend to a general protections claim under s 586 (with an alternative extension of time under s 366(2)); the Commission held the application was in substance a general protections claim filed on the wrong form and allowed the amendment.
Key holding

Although s 586 cannot be used merely to substitute a general protections cause of action for an unfair dismissal claim so as to avoid ss 725/729, the Commission may waive the irregularity and permit amendment where the initiating application was in substance a general protections claim made on the wrong approved form.

Though there is no power to amend an application to substitute a general protections cause of action for an unfair dismissal one, that does not mean that the form in which the application is made is determinative. If a party simply uses the wrong form to make one type of claim or the other, that is an irregularity that can be corrected or waived pursuant to s 586 of the Fair Work Act: Hambridge v Spotless Facilities Services Pty Ltd

Stephanie Tranquille v New Beginnings Network

21 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4103Employment & workplace
New Beginnings Network sought that Commissioner Durham recuse herself from determining its s 603 application to vary a $5,025.00 compensation order made in favour of Ms Stephanie Tranquille, alleging apprehended bias arising from case management rulings, a conciliation conference and the Commissioner's conduct of the hearing. The Commissioner heard the recusal question herself on the papers and refused it. The substantive variation application remains outstanding, with the original compliance date of 22 October 2026 unaffected.
Key holding

A Commission member should not lightly accede to a recusal application, and apprehended bias is not established unless the applicant identifies the matter said to deflect the decision-maker from the merits and articulates the logical connection between that matter and the feared departure from impartial decision-making.

It is clear from the authorities to which I have referred that I should not lightly agree to recuse myself. New Beginnings have not provided substantial grounds to warrant me doing so.

The UWU applied for bargaining orders to stop a vote on a proposed Coles subsidiary enterprise agreement, alleging CNSCE had breached the good faith bargaining requirements. Timely disclosure of an available draft enterprise agreement is relevant information required by s 228(1)(b); however, a breach does not automatically justify a bargaining order because s 230 requires the Commission to be satisfied an order is reasonable in all the circumstances.

The Civil Air Operations Officers’ Association Of Australia Trading AS Civil Air v Airservices Australia

20 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 3820Employment & workplace
Civil Air applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to arbitrate a dispute about redundancy-type benefits under the Airservices Australia (Air Traffic Control and Supporting Air Traffic Services) Enterprise Agreement 2024-2027. The dispute concerned whether air traffic controllers who cannot obtain, or refuse to obtain, a National Security Clearance or Citizenship Eligibility Waiver are entitled to cl 62.13(a)(i)-(ii) benefits on termination.
Key holding

Clause 62.13 termination benefits require the employee to be a “potentially surplus employee” under cl 62.2, and inability or refusal to obtain an NSC or CEW does not make an ATC surplus where the class of ATCs remains required.

For these reasons I do not consider that employees who are unable or refuse to obtain an NSC (or CEW) can qualify for the entitlements in clause 62.13(a)(i) and (ii) because they are in a class of employees formally identified by the Respondent as a class which has a greater number of employees in it that is necessary for its efficient and economical working, within the meaning of clause 62.2(a) of the Agreement.

The Full Bench considered an appeal from a decision to issue a certificate under s 368(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) despite Aurecon’s jurisdictional objection that Ms Baker had not been dismissed. A dismissal is not consistent with the Summary Dismissal limb of the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code where the employer’s actual reason is a performance concern rather than a belief, held on reasonable grounds at dismissal, that the employee’s conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal.

Kacy Brazier v OS MCAP Pty Ltd

19 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4043Employment & workplace
This Fair Work Commission decision concerns an order for lost pay following an earlier finding that Kacy Brazier was unfairly dismissed and an order for his reinstatement. The Commission awarded reduced lost pay under s 391 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) because Brazier made no real attempt to find paid work for most of his unemployment and performed unpaid work for his then partner. The total compensation ordered was $98,965.03 gross less tax plus $11,875.80 superannuation.
Key holding

Key holding

A specific enterprise agreement clause governing agreed overnight excursion, camp or client holiday work overrides more general agreement provisions, so the cl 6.11 entitlement of 10 hours at the applicable rate plus a sleepover allowance limits other payments, while the “applicable rate” may itself incorporate penalty or overtime rates.

Ms Ashleigh May Llewellyn v Sexyland Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1038 (16 April 2026)

16 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1038Employment & workplace
Ms Llewellyn made an unfair dismissal application under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after employment from 26 June to 27 August 2025. Because her employment was less than the minimum employment period, the Fair Work Commission dismissed the application on its own initiative under s.587. The Commission found no reasonable prospects of success.
Key holding

An unfair dismissal application cannot succeed unless the applicant has completed the minimum employment period under ss.382 and 383, and a clearly ineligible claim may be dismissed under s.587 for having no reasonable prospects.

Sections 382 and 383 of the Act provide that a person is only eligible to make an unfair dismissal application if they have completed a minimum period of employment before their dismissal.

Emma Turner v Endeavour Group Limited [2026] FWC 1318 (16 April 2026)

16 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1318Employment & workplace
Emma Turner, a casual Dan Murphy’s employee, was dismissed after ongoing incapacity following an armed robbery at work. Key holding

A dismissal for ongoing incapacity arising from a traumatic workplace incident is not unfair if the employer has a valid capacity-related reason and affords procedural fairness under s.387.

Hussnain Ali v Portier Pacific Pty Ltd T/A Uber [2026] FWC 1248 (13 April 2026)

13 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1248Employment & workplace
Mr Ali applied for an unfair deactivation remedy after Uber deactivated him in January 2026. The Commission found he was not a person protected from unfair deactivation because he had not performed regular platform work for the required six-month period. The application was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction to consider fairness.
Key holding

The Commission must determine protected status before merits, and if the applicant is not protected from unfair deactivation, it has no jurisdiction to consider fairness and cannot order a remedy.

Jessie Perrin v Yarra City Council [2026] FWC 1133 (1 April 2026)

Jessie Perrin, a casual aqua instructor, applied under s.365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) alleging Yarra City Council dismissed her by removing her from her regular Friday shift after she sought payment for set-up time. The Council objected that there was no dismissal and she remained a casual employee. The Commission found she had been dismissed at the Council’s initiative and dismissed the jurisdictional objection.
Key holding

Removing a casual employee from their regular continuing roster and replacing them can constitute termination at the employer’s initiative under s.386(1)(a), even without an express dismissal.

Objectively viewed, in circumstances where Ms Perrin had worked a regular Friday shift since early 2022, in being removed from these shifts and replaced on the roster with another member of staff, it is reasonably apparent the Respondent did not intend to offer her any future work and that her employment was being brought to an end.

Ms Duyen Ho v Persol Staffing Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1121 (1 April 2026)

1 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1121Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission dismissed an unfair dismissal application by a labour-hire chemist after her host client, PPG, barred her from its site. The Commission found she was not dismissed by her employer, Persol Staffing Australia Pty Ltd, because her employment was neither terminated at the employer's initiative nor forced by its conduct. The s.394 application therefore failed at the jurisdictional threshold.
Key holding

Under s.386, a labour-hire employee is not dismissed where the employer has not terminated employment at its initiative and has not engaged in conduct forcing the employee to resign.

More specifically, if the Applicant's employment was not terminated at the initiative of the Respondent, or if my finding is that she was not forced to resign because of conduct or a course of conduct engaged in by the Respondent, there is no jurisdictional basis for her to pursue her unfair dismissal application.

ASN Events Pty Ltd v Courtney Harris-Spencer & Michelle Harris-Spencer [2026] FWC 672 (30 March 2026)

30 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 672Employment & workplace
ASN Events Pty Ltd applied under s.120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to reduce the redundancy pay of two former finance employees by 50%, after closing its Hastings office and offering redeployment to the Melbourne CBD. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application, finding the employer had not obtained “other acceptable employment” for either employee because of significant additional travel time, travel costs and, for one employee, childcare responsibilities.
Key holding

Under s.120, alternative employment is acceptable only if it is objectively suitable considering matters including location and travelling time; significant travel and cost disadvantages can make otherwise like-for-like employment unacceptable.

Importantly, 'acceptable' requires that the alternative employment meets a relevant objective test. The test is not whether the alternative employment is identical, but requires consideration of whether the work is of a like nature, the effect of location, pay, the hours of work, workload, job security, fringe benefits, compliance with statutory conditions, seniority and the like, and not whether the employee finds the alternative employment to be acceptable.

Key holding

The Commission may dismiss an application on its own initiative under s.587 only where it is very clear there are no reasonable prospects of success and no disputed facts could affect the outcome.

An application should not be dismissed under s.587 unless it is very clear that there are no reasonable prospects of success. As such the power under s.587 is not available if there are disputed facts that could affect the outcome of the proceedings.

Tanzeel Ur Rehman v Portier Pacific Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 953 (20 March 2026)

20 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 953Employment & workplace
Tanzeel Ur Rehman was deactivated from Portier Pacific Pty Ltd’s Uber Driver Platform on 15 December 2025 and applied for an unfair deactivation remedy under s 536LU of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Portier Pacific voluntarily reactivated him on 20 February 2026 but contested any further order, including lost pay. The FWC made a formal reactivation order under s 536LQ(1) and an order for lost remuneration of $7,096.96 gross under s 536LQ(3).
Key holding

A digital labour platform operator cannot rely on voluntary reactivation, coupled with an argument that a s 536LQ(1) order has no utility, to prevent the FWC from making a formal reactivation order and an appropriate lost-pay order under s 536LQ(3).

However, that a respondent to an application under s 536LU may avert the issuance of an order to restore lost pay under s 536LQ(3) of the Act by voluntarily taking measures as referred to in s 536LQ(1) and contending that an order under s 536LQ(1) is of no utility and therefore the Commission has no basis upon which to make such order, appears contrary to the legislative intent of the provision.

The Fair Work Commission determined an application by Naomi Harnett for a suppression order under s.594 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) in relation to its earlier general protections decision in Harnett v Hands On People Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 636. The applicant sought redaction of sensitive personal and medical information after the original decision was published. The Commission made a limited suppression order, redacting some material and de-identifying some personnel.
Key holding

On a suppression application, the Commission starts from the open-justice presumption and must consider whether redacting significant parts would make the issues and reasons difficult to understand, while balancing privacy and procedural fairness.

In considering applications for an order for suppression of material; in the first instance the Commission must act on the presumption that proceedings and decisions meet the need for open justice and public scrutiny. In addition, to delete significant parts of a decision to make the matters argued and the associated reasons difficult to comprehend or record, must be taken into account.

Kellie Fitzpatrick v University of New South Wales [2026] FWC 677 (2 March 2026)

2 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 677Employment & workplace
Ms Kellie Fitzpatrick referred a dispute to the Fair Work Commission under s.65B(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after UNSW did not accept her request to change her existing hybrid part-time arrangement to work exclusively from home for three days each week. The Commission found the request was not made “because of” her eligible parent circumstance and dismissed the application. UNSW therefore had no responsive obligations under s.65A.
Key holding

Under s.65, a request for flexible working arrangements is validly made only if there is a causal connection between the employee’s eligible circumstance and the requested change.

The request made on 3 September 2025 was not validly made under s.65 of the Act.

The Fair Work Commission found that Mr Houstein, a truck driver, was dismissed rather than having genuinely resigned after a heated exchange with a leading hand on 17 June 2025. Key holding

An ostensible resignation made in the heat of the moment and not genuinely intended, where the employer ought to appreciate that, is a dismissal at the employer’s initiative under s 386.

The termination of the employment must therefore be taken to be at the employer's initiative, and is a dismissal for the purposes of section 386 of the Act.

Key holding

Under s.392(2)(c) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), remuneration for unfair dismissal compensation is broad enough to include all earnings the applicant would have received but for dismissal, including amounts claimed as subcontractor payments, so no formal finding on that characterisation is required.

Australian Workers' Union v Thales Australia Limited [2026] FWC 544 (20 February 2026)

20 Feb 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 544Employment & workplace
The Australian Workers’ Union applied under s.437 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for a protected action ballot order for certain Thales Australia Limited employees. Thales objected that the ballot questions were insufficiently clear for employees to make an informed choice, but the AWU provided amended questions at a conference. The Commission was satisfied the amended questions were clear and that all s.443(1) requirements were met, and a protected action ballot order was made.
Key holding

The Commission may make a protected action ballot order where it is satisfied of the s.443(1) requirements, including that there is a notification time and that the applicant has been, and is, genuinely trying to reach agreement.

On the basis of the material before me, including the declaration of Mick Ivill, Organiser, setting out the steps taken by the AWU in bargaining with the Employer and that it has been, and is, genuinely trying to reach agreement with Thales, I am satisfied that there is a notification time in relation to the proposed agreement and that all of the requirements in s.443(1) of the Act have been met.

Agustina Rodriguez v Elena Stevens; Michael George Stevens [2026] FWC 550 (20 February 2026)

20 Feb 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 550Employment & workplace
Ms Rodriguez filed a general protections application four days out of time after the Commission advised she withdraw earlier unfair dismissal and general protections applications because s.725 barred two applications about the same dismissal. The Fair Work Commission accepted the circumstances were exceptional and granted an extension of time. The substantive general protections dispute can now proceed.
Key holding

The Commission may grant an extension of time for a late general protections application where the delay is caused by the need to withdraw overlapping applications under s.725, because those circumstances can be exceptional.

The Commission may exercise its discretion to allow a further period for a general protections application to be made if it is satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances. I consider the circumstances set out above to be exceptional circumstances that warrant an extension of time.

Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance v Australian Broadcasting Corporation [2026] FWC 537 (20 February 2026)

20 Feb 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 537Employment & workplace
The MEAA applied to the Fair Work Commission under s.437 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for a protected action ballot order covering certain ABC employees. The ABC did not object, and the Commission was satisfied the statutory requirements were met. Deputy President Hampton made the order, appointed TrueVote as ballot agent, set voting to close on 10 March 2026, and referred the matter for a s.448A compulsory conciliation conference.
Key holding

A protected action ballot order under s.437 may be made where the Commission is satisfied there is a notification time and that all requirements in s.443(1) are met, including that the applicant has been and is genuinely trying to reach agreement.

On the basis of the material before me, including the declaration of Cassandra Carmel Derrick, MEEA Media Section Director, setting out the steps taken by the MEAA in bargaining with the Employer and that it has been, and is, genuinely trying to reach agreement with the ABC, I am satisfied that there is a notification time in relation to the proposed agreement and that all of the requirements in s.443(1) of the Act have been met.

Jason Nikora v Black Cat Civil [2026] FWC 553 (20 February 2026)

20 Feb 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 553Employment & workplace
Jason Nikora applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), alleging unfair dismissal by Black Cat Civil after his summary dismissal on 16 July 2025 for alleged speeding, an airport altercation and urinating at camp. Commissioner Simpson found valid reasons based on repeated speeding and the Moranbah Airport altercation, despite procedural deficiencies in the investigation. The application was dismissed.
Key holding

Repeated on-site safety breaches and connected off-duty misconduct can together constitute a valid reason for dismissal.

The conduct in relation to speeding and the misconduct at the Moranbah Airport taken together were a valid reason for dismissal.

Betina Unterstell v Ventia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 549 (20 February 2026)

20 Feb 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 549Employment & workplace
Ms Unterstell lodged an unfair dismissal application on 26 November 2025, almost five months after resigning from Ventia Pty Ltd on 29 May 2025. Ventia objected that she voluntarily resigned and that the application was out of time. The Fair Work Commission found no exceptional circumstances and dismissed the application.
Key holding

The Commission may extend time under s 394(3) only if, after weighing all statutory considerations as a whole, it is satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist.

In weighing the considerations in s. 394(3) of the Act as a whole, I am not satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist.
